## TL;DR

Addressed review rounds 1 and 2 by adding Releases, Deployments, and Checks to the rendered contrast audit matrix. Built the app and reran `bun run contrast:audit` with headless WebKit. It passed across 16 theme scopes and 17 screen states, examining 17,282 visible text runs with no text below the WCAG floor. Updated the QA record with the latest results.

## Work and rationale

The review findings identified missing main page states in the audit: Releases and Deployments first, then Checks. The router exposes `/releases`, `/deployments`, and `/checks`, and the November QA note names Checks among the main work surfaces. A separate layout pass does not establish text contrast, so I extended the rendered audit’s own screen list.

In `makeScreens`, I added one screen state for each real route, using the same `gotoApp` preparation as the existing pages. That keeps page coverage within the existing fixture server and sends all visible text through the existing contrast probe for every configured theme scope. No new contrast logic, thresholds, token values, fixture-specific exemptions, or `repoos.toml` changes were needed.

After adding Releases and Deployments, the audit passed at 16 scopes × 16 states. After adding Checks, I rebuilt with `bun run build` and reran the audit. The final result was 16 scopes × 17 screen states, with 17,282 visible text runs examined. There were zero contrast failures. The probe separately classified 320 exempt runs, 64 disabled-component runs, zero invisible runs, 9,265 gradient worst-stop judgments, and 20 unchecked gradient-logo runs using `background-clip: text`. I preserved those distinctions in the report; unchecked logo text is a stated probe limitation, not a measured pass or a finding.

Updated `docs/qa/2026-11-theme-contrast-qa.md` to name Checks, Releases, and Deployments and replace the earlier counts with the final run’s output. No color changes were warranted by this evidence, and no new exemptions were introduced.

## Approaches tried

I compared the reviewer findings with the router and `makeScreens`. The existing screen states already used direct route navigation for pages such as Agents, Settings, Dev, and Context, so the three missing pages could be represented as concise named entries following that established approach. I then used the rendered audit rather than relying on a layout-only browser pass, because the audit evaluates actual rendered text against computed backgrounds and gradient stops.

I built once after changing the audit source so the launcher used current compiled output, then ran the full rendered audit over the configured themes. The results confirmed every newly added route was prepared as part of the 17-state matrix; the command completed without unavailable-state warnings and passed with zero below-floor runs.

## Challenges and blockers

The challenge was reconciling the broad “main pages” wording with the actual enumerated screen matrix. The existing QA note made clear that Checks needed rendered coverage, and the follow-up review caught this gap even after Releases and Deployments had been added. Updating the matrix and then checking the emitted state count and total text runs provides direct evidence that coverage increased.

The audit does not measure every visual element. Its output explicitly marks gradient-clipped logo text as unchecked, and it retains the established collapsed board column exemption for text overlaying status gradients. Neither category was expanded or relabeled as a pass during this update.

## Key learnings

A QA record should name the exact rendered state matrix and tie its coverage claim to the audit output. Router presence or a separate responsive layout pass is not enough to claim contrast coverage. Adding each main route to the existing matrix ensures it is probed across all configured theme scopes with the same rendered contrast criteria. For this run, 17 states across 16 dark/light theme scopes passed, and the record now reflects that evidence precisely.
